newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Silent marchers protest Argentine newsman's murder.
newsitem.headline: Silent marchers protest Argentine newsman's murder.

text.p: Thousands of Argentines marched in silence through Buenos Aires on Wednesday in a show of solidarity with the colleagues of a news photographer whose murder this weekend recalled the death squads of the 1970s.

Journalists and photographers wearing black ribbons were joined by politicians, human rights groups and members of the public in a rally to demand an answer to the question on their banners: "Who killed Jose Luis Cabezas?"

The body of Cabezas, a 35-year-old photographer for the top-selling weekly news magazine Noticias, was found in a car on a dirt track outside the beach resort of Pinamar, southeast of Buenos Aires, early on Saturday.

He had been handcuffed, shot in the head, doused with fuel and set on fire, probably while he was still alive. His corpse was so badly burned it could only be identified by his car keys, watch and dental records.
The brutal killing chilled Argentina, a gruesome reminder of the thousands of death squad killings before and after the coup of 1976 that started seven years of brutal military rule.

"It seems to me Argentina's society is sending a message that we don't want any more anonymous mafias killing people in the streets without motives," Noticias Editor Hector D'Amico said when the midday march ended in a rally in the Plaza de Mayo, outside President Carlos Menem's government house.
"If the message is left unchallenged that you can put a stop to an idea or a story by killing a journalist, it will be a tragedy for democracy," D'Amico told reporters.
Police have launched a huge investigation with a $300,000 reward, and investigating Judge Jose Luis Macchi said on Wednesday he had interviewed a witness "who could be fundamental."
But so far most suspicion has fallen on the very Buenos Aires Province police force handling the investigation.

Noticias is critical of Menem's Peronist government and has also had scoops on corruption cases including revelations of crime syndicates in the Buenos Aires police that forced provincial Governor Eduardo Duhalde to purge its ranks.
Duhalde, calling the murder "an attack on the system itself," said the idea that his own police could be involved "stops me from sleeping."

"We must have an investigation that is not suspected of complicity," said the opposition Frepaso coalition's leader Carlos "Chacho" Alvarez. Radical Party leader Rodolfo Terragno was even more outspoken: "You cannot have foxes investigating a massacre in a hen-house."
Interior Minister Carlos Corach, while condemning the killing as "an attack on the freedom of the press," said he did not want the case to be used for political ends.
